title: A DVR keeps its normalized order after extending its residue field
statement: Let k be an algebraically closed field, let k' be an extension field of k [def-pc-field-extension], and let (R, m) be a discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring] which is a k-algebra with residue-field identification R/m = k. Write K for the fraction field of R. Put R' = (R\otimes_k k')_{m(R\otimes_k k')} and let K' be the fraction field of the domain K\otimes_k k'. Then R' is a discrete valuation ring, the image of every uniformizer of R is a uniformizer of R', and for every nonzero f\in K the normalized exponent of f in R' equals its normalized exponent in R.

source.place: Lemma 00PD (algebra-lemma-characterize-dvr), characterization by a principal maximal ideal and unique unit-times-uniformizer factorization; after the stated residue-field extension, the tensor/localization and exponent calculation is elementary

proof.text: Choose a uniformizer $t$ of $R$, so $\mathfrak m=tR$ [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring]. Since $R/\mathfrak m=k$ and $k'$ is a field extension of $k$ [def-pc-field-extension], tensoring the exact sequence $0\to\mathfrak m\to R\to k\to0$ over $k$ with $k'$ (exact, as $k$ is a field) identifies $(R\otimes_k k')/t(R\otimes_k k')$ with $k\otimes_k k'=k'$, a field. Hence $\mathfrak m(R\otimes_k k')=t(R\otimes_k k')$ is a maximal ideal, and the localization $R'$ is a local ring with maximal ideal generated by the image of $t$ and residue field $k'$.

proof.text: Let $f\in K^\times$. By the factorization in $R$ [lem-weil-pbc-dvr-unit-times-uniformizer-power] applied to a numerator and denominator of $f$, write $f=ut^n$ with $u\in R^\times$ and $n\in\mathbf Z$. The image of $u$ in $R'$ is a unit because its residue in $k$ is nonzero and hence remains nonzero in $k'$. Therefore $f=ut^n$ in the fraction field of $R'$, with $u\in R'^\times$ and $t$ a uniformizer of $R'$ by the previous step, so by the definition of the normalized exponent the exponent of $f$ in $R'$ is $n$, which is its exponent in $R$.
